label: Lost the fight
title: Two Generals, One Printing Press
dek: After Yorktown, the two senior British commanders spent years arguing in print about whose fault it was. One of them figured out you can win an argument by leaving it.
summary: After the 1781 British surrender at Yorktown, generals Henry Clinton and Charles Cornwallis traded blame in a 1783 pamphlet war.

blocks.text: His case: Cornwallis marched out of the Carolinas into Virginia on his own initiative, then dug in at Yorktown, a spot that became a trap the moment a French fleet took the Chesapeake. Which it did.
His case: Clinton was the boss. His letters said to hold a naval post on the Chesapeake, and Cornwallis read them as orders to stay put and wait for ships. The ships sailed after he’d surrendered.
All four fought in 1783, in print. Titles shortened. The originals are much, much longer.

items: I. Clinton, The Narrative. Opening shot: Virginia was Cornwallis’s idea. Several editions that year.
II. Cornwallis, An Answer. Replies only to the parts about Cornwallis. Relief by sea was promised. It was late.
III. Clinton, Observations. A reply to the reply. Historically, not a winning move.
IV. “Themistocles,” A Reply. An anonymous pamphleteer lists Clinton’s “numerous errors.” Cornwallis gets a cornerman.

blocks.text: Clinton spent his last years revising a much longer account of his whole command. It came out in 1954. A collector had already reprinted six of the pamphlets in 1888, which is more than most arguments get.
Clinton kept writing. Cornwallis kept getting promoted.
Cornwallis won the argument by never needing to have it.

sources: Benjamin Franklin Stevens, ed., The Campaign in Virginia, 1781: An Exact Reprint of Six Rare Pamphlets on the Clinton-Cornwallis Controversy (1888).
William B. Willcox, ed., The American Rebellion (1954).
